body: Hello. Over the next three months, a daily note will help you become someone who drinks less, at your own pace. This is not medical advice; if stopping feels hard or unsafe, please speak to a doctor first.
Start with curiosity, not rules. Today, just notice when you think about having a drink and what was happening right before.
You do not need a dramatic reason to drink less. Wanting clearer mornings or more money is reason enough.
Write down three things you hope will feel different if you drink less. Keep the list; you will come back to it.
Pick one alcohol-free drink you genuinely like the taste of and keep some at home. Having an easy alternative matters.
Many people drink to change how they feel. Today, name the feeling you most often want to change: stress, boredom, shyness?
Choose one evening this week to have no alcohol at all. Notice how you sleep and how you feel the next morning.
You do not owe anyone an explanation for what is in your glass. A simple not tonight, thanks is a full answer.
Notice the habits around drinking: a certain chair, a certain time, a certain friend. Habits live in places as much as in people.
If your week ends with a drink on Friday, try starting it with something else: a walk, a bath, a favourite meal.
Cravings usually rise and fall within about twenty minutes. If one arrives today, set a timer and do something else until it passes.
Drinking less is a skill, and skills improve with practice. A slip is information, not a verdict on who you are.
Count what you spend on alcohol in a typical week. Then decide what you would like that money to do for you instead.
Tell one person you trust that you are cutting back. Saying it out loud makes it easier to keep.
At your next social event, hold a glass of something you enjoy. Having something in your hand quiets most questions.
Notice how much of the pleasure of a drink is in the first sip. Ask whether the second and third bring the same.
Plan one rewarding thing for the evening hours you used to drink in. Fill the time, or the old habit will.
If someone teases you for not drinking, it often says more about their habits than about yours. Smile and move on.
Today, write a short sentence about the person you are becoming: someone who chooses when and whether to drink.
Hangovers steal mornings. Picture one weekend morning this month spent fully awake and enjoying yourself.
Find one place to unwind that does not revolve around alcohol: a café, a cinema, a park, a class.
Stress will still arrive. Make a short list of other ways you can take the edge off: a call, a shower, music, a stretch.
Notice how you feel on days without a drink. Some people find more energy; others find feelings they had been muting. Both are useful to know.
Choose one simple rule for this week, such as no drinking at home or not before eight. Simple rules are easier to keep.
When you do drink, try alternating with water. It slows the pace and helps you notice when you have had enough.
Be gentle with yourself about past drinking. You made choices with what you knew. Today you know more.
Look for alcohol-free versions of things you love: a beer, a spritz, a ritual. Many people find the ritual matters more than the alcohol.
Make a plan before an event: how many drinks, if any, and when you will leave. Deciding in advance is easier than deciding in the moment.
Notice what alcohol adverts and social media suggest about relaxing and fun. You are allowed to define those things for yourself.
Celebrate a small win today. One evening without alcohol, or one drink fewer, is real progress.
If boredom is a trigger, write down five things you could do on a dull evening. Put the list somewhere easy to see.
Some friendships may feel different as you change. Notice which ones feel just as warm without a drink between you.
Try a morning activity this weekend that you would have skipped after a late night: a market, a swim, a long breakfast.
Feeling awkward without a drink at a party is common at first. Awkwardness fades with practice, like any new skill.
Write down how you feel right now, honestly. Tracking moods for a few weeks can show you patterns no one else would notice.
Remember, the goal is yours to set. Drinking less, drinking rarely or not drinking at all are all valid choices.
Notice the voice that says you deserve a drink. Ask what else you might deserve: rest, kindness, a treat that leaves no fog.
Plan an evening with a friend that is built around something other than drinking: a film, a game, a cooking night.
If you slip, look at what led up to it without blame. Tired, hungry, lonely and stressed are common doorways.
Check in with your list of hopes from the first week. Has anything on it begun to shift?
Learn to recognise the moment when one drink would turn into several. Name it, and decide what you want to do there.
You may sleep more deeply or wake more clearly after a few dry nights. Notice what your own body tells you.
Rehearse a friendly line for when someone offers you a drink. Having it ready takes the pressure off.
Halfway point. Take a minute to notice how your evenings, mornings and spending have changed.
If you live with someone who drinks, talk kindly about what would help you, such as keeping less at home.
Change the route that leads you past your usual off-licence or bar, if it is a common trigger.
Notice how good it feels to remember the whole of a night out. Clear memories are a quiet gift.
Drinking less does not make you boring. Many people find they become more present, funny and engaged.
Try a new hobby this month that uses your hands or your mind in the evenings. Curiosity is a good replacement for routine.
If anxiety rises when you drink less, be patient with it. Alcohol can mask nerves, and you are learning other ways to calm them.
Write down one reason you are glad you started this. Read it before your next social event.
Stock your kitchen with snacks and drinks for the time of day you used to reach for alcohol.
You do not need to label yourself to make changes. Just be someone who is paying attention.
Today, do something kind for your body that alcohol used to crowd out: an early night, a proper meal, a walk.
Be ready for comments like just one won't hurt. You can agree and still say no.
Notice whether drinking less has changed your mood the next day. Many people find they are steadier.
If a big occasion is coming up, decide now how you want to remember it. Then plan your choices around that memory.
Find one community, online or in person, where people share alcohol-free ideas. Belonging makes change easier.
Treat yourself with something you have saved for by drinking less. Let the reward be visible.
You are rewriting a habit that may have taken years to form. Progress may be gradual, and that is fine.
If you usually drink while cooking, try sparkling water with a slice of lemon in a nice glass instead.
When you feel left out of a toast, raise whatever you are holding. Joining in is about the moment, not the contents.
Notice what you do with your hands and mouth in social settings. A drink, a snack, a story: what helps you feel at ease?
Talk to yourself the way a supportive friend would if you had a hard evening.
Try a week of noting each drink you have, with no judgement. Awareness is often enough to change the pattern.
Think of a time you felt truly relaxed without alcohol. What was around you? Can you recreate some of it?
If you are drinking to cope with grief, stress or pain, please consider talking to a professional. You do not have to manage alone.
Let yourself enjoy the clarity of a sober evening: the conversation, the food, the drive home.
Remember to eat well and drink water when you do drink. Taking care of yourself is never all or nothing.
Notice the people who respect your choices without fuss. They are good company for this journey.
Plan your next holiday or celebration with a few alcohol-free treats in mind. Novelty helps habits change.
If a slip happens, restart the next day without waiting for Monday or a new month. Every day is a fine day to begin again.
Reflect on what you have learned about your own triggers. That knowledge will serve you for years.
Try something new today that you would have been too tired or foggy to do before.
Your confidence in social situations is growing, even if slowly. Notice one moment of ease this week.
Consider sharing your experience with someone who is curious about drinking less. Your story may help.
Decide what role, if any, you want alcohol to have in your life going forward. It is your choice to make.
Notice how much more time you have on evenings and weekends. Choose one meaningful way to use it.
Write down one thing that is easier now than it was two months ago.
Being sober curious is about choice, not fear. Keep choosing what makes your days better.
Remember your reasons when old patterns call. They are still true.
Think about the mornings you have won back. What has been the best one so far?
Spend a little time thinking about the life you want, not just the habit you want to change.
Notice one way you are kinder to yourself now than when you began.
Plan a small celebration for the end of these ninety days, one that fits the person you are becoming.
Look back at your list of three hopes. Which have come true, even a little?
Keep the tools that worked: the alternative drink, the ready answer, the evening plan, the honest friend.
Changing your relationship with alcohol often ripples into other areas. Notice where else you have grown.
Be proud of every choice you made with intention, whether it was a drink or a no.
Look back over these weeks. What surprised you most about drinking less?
You started with curiosity and built new habits from it. That same curiosity can guide your next change.
This is the last note. You have become someone who chooses whether and when to drink, and that freedom is yours to keep.
